revolutionary-battles-1775-1776.works: The opening view and the Massachusetts bookmark read at once: red and blue diamonds against a short legend, colony names printed on the map, and the Lexington and Concord pop-up puts April 19, 1775 right under the title. With Key Port Cities on, the circled anchors for the five major ports (Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk, Charleston) stand out clearly from the small anchors, so the ports question can be answered by eye.

findings.where: q2-colony and q2-colony-ny views; Thirteen British Colonies (Colony Area); Q2 'Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?', step 3
findings.what: I click inside Virginia, then New York, to read the colony name as the sheet says, and nothing opens. Most colony names are printed on the map, but Rhode Island has no label when zoomed out and nothing anywhere says Quebec.
findings.why: Thirty kids clicking and getting nothing means hands up and me walking the room in a 15-minute question. This is the step that tells them which colony each battle was in, and the answer notes expect Rhode Island and Quebec.
findings.suggestion: Turn on a Colony Area pop-up titled with the colony name (the About text says it has one) and add a 'Quebec (British province)' label; or change step 3 to 'Read the colony name printed on the map'.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony.png and --q2-colony-ny.png: '(no pop-up opened)'; --q2-colony.png shows no Rhode Island or Quebec label.

findings.where: q1-bookmark and q4-circles views; Turning Points drawn over Revolutionary War Battles (and Key Port Cities, still on from Q3); Q1 step 4 (Boston diamond); Q4 steps 3-4 (Fort Washington, Fort Lee, Trenton)
findings.what: At the Massachusetts bookmark I can't find a 'Boston diamond': circle 2 sits where Boston is, and the only other diamond nearby is a blue one out on the coast to the north-east, which isn't Boston. Zoomed in on New York, circle 4 sits on northern Manhattan (clicking it gives '1 of 5') and circle 5 sits on Trenton. There isn't a single blue diamond in that view, so I can't see Trenton's colour, and colour is the only place the winner is shown. The big New York port anchor sits on top of circle 3 as well.
findings.why: The sheet makes colour the only source for who won, so a hidden diamond means a blank or a guess. Kids will also click the coastal diamond for Boston and copy the wrong dates.
findings.suggestion: Move the Turning Points circles to sit beside the battle they mark (or draw them as a ring behind the diamond) so each diamond's colour shows. Label Boston, Concord, Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton at bookmark zoom. Make 'Turn off Key Port Cities' the first step of Q4.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-bookmark.png (circle 2 over Boston, blue diamond on the coast to the NE); --q4-circles.png (circles 4 and 5 over the battles, no blue diamond visible); --q4-circle4.png pop-up '1 of 5'.

findings.where: q2-all, q2-colony and q2-colony-ny views; Revolutionary War Battles; Q2 step 1 ('Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina')
findings.what: If I zoom out far enough to get South Carolina in, the Quebec diamond drops off the top of the screen, and with the legend open the panel covers New England. When Quebec is in view, the Carolinas aren't. To get both I'd have to zoom out another step, where the diamonds around New York already overlap.
findings.why: The answer notes expect Quebec for 1775. Kids who never see it will miss it, and I'd lose minutes getting everyone onto the same view.
findings.suggestion: Add an 'All battles 1775-1776' bookmark framed from Quebec City to Charleston, leaving room for the legend panel, and label Quebec on the map.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-all.png and --q2-colony.png (Quebec diamond not in view, Carolinas in view); --q2-colony-ny.png and --open.png (Quebec at the top, Carolinas off the bottom).

findings.where: q2-all and q2-bunkerhill views; Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups; Q2 step 2 (read each diamond's year)
findings.what: The year is only in the pop-ups, so 21 diamonds means 21 clicks, and zoomed out, one click near Boston gives '1 of 3' to page through.
findings.why: This should be the two-minute 'look how the war moved' moment on a map. Instead it becomes 15 minutes of clicking and copying, and it's where the period runs over.
findings.suggestion: Show the year on the map, for example outlined diamonds for 1775 and filled for 1776 (keeping red and blue for the winner), or a small year label on each diamond, so the shift from 1775 to 1776 can be seen at a glance.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-bunkerhill.png pop-up '1 of 3'; --q2-colony.png (diamonds overlapping around New York).

findings.where: q3-port view; Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781; Reading the map and Q3 step 4 ('The layer has no pop-ups')
findings.what: The sheet and the About text both say the port layer has no pop-ups, but clicking a port opened one: 'Stonington, CT'.
findings.why: That actually helps the kids, but the sheet tells them to work the names out from the coastline, which is slower. And when the sheet is wrong about the map, I trust the rest of it less.
findings.suggestion: If every major port's pop-up gives its name, change Q3 step 4 to 'Click a port to read its name' and drop the 'no pop-ups' lines. If not, switch the pop-ups off so the sheet is true.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q3-port.png, pop-up text: 'Stonington, CT'.

findings.where: q1-lexington view; Lexington and Concord pop-up; Q1 step 5 (Measure Boston to Concord)
findings.what: The pop-up says Concord is '20 miles northwest of Boston', but the answer notes want about 16 miles from Measure (accept 15 to 17).
findings.why: Sharp kids will write 20 straight from the pop-up, or ask in front of the class why their measurement is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Change the pop-up to give the straight-line figure, or add a note to the answers: 'The pop-up's 20 miles is not a straight line. Accept 15 to 17 from Measure.' I'd check which figure the source gives before choosing.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-lexington.png pop-up: '...stored in Concord, Massachusetts, 20 miles northwest of Boston.'

findings.where: q1-lexington and q2-bunkerhill views; selected-feature highlight; Q1 steps 2-3, Q2 step 3, Q4 step 4
findings.what: When I click a diamond it turns light blue while the pop-up is open, so I can't check its red or blue against the legend until I close the pop-up.
findings.why: Colour is the only way to read the winner, and a light-blue highlight next to the blue 'American Victory' swatch invites the wrong answer.
findings.suggestion: Change the highlight to an outline that leaves the fill colour visible, or add to Reading the map: 'Note the diamond's colour before you click it.'
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-lexington.png and --q2-bunkerhill.png (the selected diamond is drawn cyan).

roads-trails-and-rails-west.works: The opening view shows all seven trails fanning out from Missouri at a glance, which nearly answers 'where did the trails begin?' before anyone clicks, and every pop-up is titled with the trail's name. With Railroads on, the thick transcontinental lines over the dotted trails, plus a gray line's pop-up ('Union Pacific (Transcontinental)... 1869'), make the trails-to-rails comparison plain.

findings.where: open and q3-indigenous views; Trails West legend; Q1 step 1, Q2 step 1, Q3 step 3
findings.what: Oregon and California are two nearly identical olive dot colours, and Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish and Pony Express are all very dark. Along the Platte, four of them run on top of each other. I can't tell which is which from the legend.
findings.why: The sheet sends kids to the legend first. They'll guess, and I'll end up telling the room to click instead.
findings.suggestion: Give the seven trails clearly different colours that work for colour-blind students, and label each trail by name along its line.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--open.png; --q3-indigenous.png.

findings.where: q2-oregon view; Trails West pop-ups; Q2 step 2 ('Click the Oregon Trail')
findings.what: I clicked the Oregon Trail and the pop-up that opened was the Pony Express Trail, '1 of 4'.
findings.why: Kids who don't page through will copy the Pony Express's 1,800 miles as the Oregon Trail's length. The answer looks right and is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Reword step 2: 'Click the Oregon Trail in Idaho or Oregon, where it runs on its own, and check that the pop-up title says Oregon Trail.' Or add an Oregon Trail bookmark at that spot.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q2-oregon.png, pop-up title 'Pony Express Trail', '1 of 4'.

findings.where: open and q2-oregon views; basemap labels; Q2 steps 3-4 (Measure Independence to Portland)
findings.what: At the zooms I can see, the basemap labels Kansas City but not Independence, and the opening view labels Seattle and San Francisco but not Portland. I can't tell whether they appear when zoomed in closer.
findings.why: Measure needs both ends in sight, and hunting for Portland eats minutes. Kansas City is near enough to land inside the 1,450-1,550 range, so it isn't fatal.
findings.suggestion: Add a small labelled point layer for the trail ends (Independence, St. Joseph, Nauvoo, Portland, Sacramento, Santa Fe), or word step 4 as 'from the trail's eastern end at Kansas City to its western end at Portland'.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q2-oregon.png (Kansas City labelled, no Independence); --open.png (no Portland label).

findings.where: q3-indigenous view; Indigenous Territories; Q3 steps 2-4 ('Whose land?')
findings.what: With Indigenous Territories on, the shading stops at straight lines: nothing west of a vertical line through Wyoming, nothing south of a line across Nebraska. Long stretches of the trail run across unshaded land.
findings.why: The question asks whether the land was empty. If kids see blank land beside the trail, the map says the opposite of the answer I want. It may just be tiles still loading when the picture was taken, but school wifi could do the same thing.
findings.suggestion: Test the layer on a school Chromebook on the school network. If it loads in tiles, add 'wait for the colours to fill in' to step 2, or use a lighter version of the layer. Add a bookmark on the Oregon Trail at the zoom where the names appear.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q3-indigenous.png (straight-edged gaps around Rock Springs and south of the Cheyenne-to-Kearney stretch).

findings.where: q3-indigenous view; Indigenous Territories labels (no pop-up); Q3 step 4 ('Find two nations whose land it crossed')
findings.what: Only a few names show: Tsésthoe (Cheyenne), Sicangu, Oohenumpa and a Ponca label. They sit in the middle of their areas, away from the trail. The areas the trail actually runs through in this view have no name in sight, the see-through colours blend where they overlap, and there's no pop-up to click. Sicangu and Oohenumpa have no English name with them, so I can't match them to what I teach.
findings.why: Kids can't tell whose land a stretch of trail is on, so they'll write down any two names on screen. If one asks what Sicangu is, I don't have an answer ready.
findings.suggestion: Turn on a pop-up that gives the nation's name with its common English name (for example 'Sicangu (Lakota)'), and label each area more than once so a name shows near the trail at this zoom.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q3-indigenous.png.

findings.where: q4-railroads view; Railroads 1826 to 1911 and Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911; Q4 steps 1-2
findings.what: The sheet's 'thin gray lines' show up as a dense black mesh that buries the dotted trails east of the Rockies. At laptop size the legend cuts off at Central Pacific, so I'd have to scroll to find Southern Pacific, whose colour is close to the orange Butterfield trail.
findings.why: Kids need to see the thick transcontinental lines against the trails. The black mesh turns that into zooming and squinting.
findings.suggestion: Lighten Railroads 1826 to 1911 to a pale gray to match the sheet, and add a Nebraska-to-Utah bookmark where the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines can be compared with the trails.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q4-railroads.png.

us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850.works: The four shades show the North-South split at a glance, with the free-to-slave line along Pennsylvania's southern border and the Ohio River obvious, and the solid black routes visibly run from Virginia down to the Gulf. One click on a state gives its name and year, and the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark shows the orange routes and town names clearly.

findings.where: q2-line view; Missouri Compromise Line over US States and Territories 1850; Q2 steps 1-2 ('Click it and read its pop-up')
findings.what: I clicked the gray dashed Missouri Compromise Line and got the 'Unorganized Territory' pop-up instead, with no '1 of 2' to page to the line. The line runs along the edge of that territory, so the click lands on the territory.
findings.why: Kids never see the line's own pop-up: its title, 'Enacted 1820', or the note that Missouri was the exception. They may still write 1820 from the territory pop-up, but only by luck, and they miss the 'why does it matter' part.
findings.suggestion: Make the line easier to hit (thicker, drawn above the states, with a wider click area), or put the 1820 note into the Missouri pop-up as well. Then add to step 2: 'Check the pop-up title says Missouri Compromise Line.'
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q2-line.png, pop-up: 'Unorganized Territory... would not permit the enslavement of people in 1820... Free by Missouri Compromise'.

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania view; US States and Territories 1850 pop-up; Q1 step 3 (read what year each became free or slave); front step 2
findings.what: Pennsylvania, the first state I'd click in front of the class, contradicts itself. It says it 'passed legislation against the enslavement of people 1780', then that the source records it as 'Abolition by state action between 1830-1850'.
findings.why: Kids will write 1780, 1830 or 1850, and I'll have to explain on the spot why the map disagrees with itself.
findings.suggestion: Fix the text, for example 'passed a law in 1780 to end slavery gradually', and either drop the 1830-1850 class line or explain it ('the 1920 map groups it with...'). I'd check the Harper's class for Pennsylvania first.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q1-pennsylvania.png, pop-up text as quoted.

findings.where: open and q3-slavetrade views (no labels); q2-line view (zoomed labels); basemap; Q1, Q3 steps 2-4, Q4 step 2
findings.what: At the opening zoom there isn't a single state or river name on the map. Names only appear when I zoom in, and they're modern ones (Oklahoma, Colorado, Wyoming) printed over 1850 territories. The Ohio River the sheet mentions isn't labelled.
findings.why: Every 'where' answer depends on clicking states one by one, and kids will copy 'Oklahoma' for land that wasn't a state in 1850.
findings.suggestion: Add a label layer with the 1850 state and territory names, and label the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png and --q3-slavetrade.png (no names); --q2-line.png (OKLAHOMA, COLORADO, WYOMING labels).

findings.where: q4-bookmark view; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes and Cities; Q4 steps 1-3 ('Where do the routes lead?')
findings.what: With the legend open, the panel covers eastern Ohio and the Lake Erie shore. The towns the answer notes name, Cleveland and Ashtabula, are under it, Chatham is cut in half, and Toronto and Montreal are off the screen. Chicago, Detroit and St. Louis are each labelled twice, once in orange and once in gray.
findings.why: The point of the question is 'they kept going into Canada', and the bookmark stops just short of Canada.
findings.suggestion: Widen the bookmark, or move it east and north, so it takes in Lake Erie and southern Ontario with the legend open. Or add a second bookmark, 'Routes into Canada'.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q4-bookmark.png.

findings.where: open view legend; Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade; Reading the map
findings.what: The legend says 'Route of L'Amistead'. The sheet says the Amistad.
findings.why: It's a small thing, but kids copy spellings from the legend, and it looks careless.
findings.suggestion: Rename the legend class to 'Route of the Amistad'.
findings.evidence: Legend text: 'Route of L'Amistead'.

findings.where: open view; US States and Territories 1850 shades; Q1 steps 1-2
findings.what: The brown and green are both muted and about equally dark, and the two paler 'by compromise' shades are close to each other.
findings.why: A couple of my students are colour-blind every year, and brown against green is the pair they can't separate.
findings.suggestion: Make free and slave clearly different in lightness, or add a hatch pattern to the slave groups, and check the shades with a colour-blindness simulator.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png.

civil-war-battlefields.works: The 1863 states layer does the heavy lifting: blue Union, brown Confederacy, state names printed and the white dashed boundary clear. Zoomed to Washington, Maryland's paler border-state shade against Virginia's tan, with the boundary running along the Potomac, answers the border-states question in seconds. Diamond size makes Gettysburg and Antietam jump out.

findings.where: q3-railroads view (also the open and q2-dc views); Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static); Q3 'Railroads, North and South', steps 2-3
findings.what: I turned the states off and zoomed in on the boundary as the sheet says, and there are no railroads at all, just the basemap and diamonds. There are none at the opening view or zoomed to Washington either. The dark gray lines only appear much closer in, in the Antietam view, a couple of hundred miles across, where North and South can't be compared.
findings.why: The whole question is comparing the two networks. With nothing on screen it's dead, and the answer notes don't say what zoom to use.
findings.suggestion: Set the railroad layer's visible range so it draws at the whole-East zoom, from the Atlantic to the Mississippi (or publish a simplified copy for that scale). Add a 'Railroads in 1863' bookmark at that zoom and name it in Q3 step 1.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png (no railroads); --open.png and --q2-dc.png (none); --q4-diamond.png (thin dark lines appear only at this close zoom).

findings.where: q3-railroads view; Boundary between Union and Confederacy; Q3 step 1 (find the white dashed boundary, with the states layer off)
findings.what: With the states layer off, the white dashed boundary almost vanishes against the pale basemap. I can just make out a faint dash line across the left of the view.
findings.why: Kids can't compare north and south of a line they can't find.
findings.suggestion: Give the boundary a dark outline so it shows on both the shaded states and the plain basemap, or swap the steps so students switch the states layer off only after they've found the line.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png.

findings.where: q2-dc and q4-diamond views; Civil War Battlefield Boundary (tan areas) under Civil War Battlefields; Q4 steps 1-2 ('Click the tan shaded areas')
findings.what: At the Virginia zoom the sheet starts with, I see diamonds but no tan areas. Closer in, the battlefield areas are pale shapes almost the same colour as Virginia's tan, and the diamonds sit on top of them, so my clicks hit the diamonds.
findings.why: Kids will click diamonds or empty tan and wonder where the battlefields are. The step is fiddly in exactly the state with the most battles.
findings.suggestion: Give the battlefield areas a darker fill or outline that shows on both the tan and the blue shades. Or let students click the diamonds, whose pop-ups give the name, and say so on the sheet.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png (no tan areas visible); --q4-diamond.png (pale areas on tan Virginia).

findings.where: q4-gettysburg view; Civil War Core Areas / Battlefield Boundary pop-up; Q4 steps 2-3
findings.what: The Gettysburg pop-up (1 of 2) gives only the name and '14,508 acres'. There's no state, though the About text says it shows a state code, and the answer notes say 73,551 acres. At that zoom the diamonds are gone and no state names show, so the only clue to the state is the blue background.
findings.why: 'Name a battle in a Union state' depends on knowing the state. If I read the acres out from the answer notes, they won't match what the kids see.
findings.suggestion: Add the state to both pop-ups. Change the answer notes to say the first pop-up may be the core area (14,508 acres) and the arrows lead to the full boundary.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q4-gettysburg.png, pop-up: 'GETTYSBURG... It spans 14,508 acres.' '1 of 2'.

findings.where: open and q2-dc views; Civil War Battlefields symbols and legend; Reading the map
findings.what: Navy 'Union Victory' diamonds sit on navy Union states (Gettysburg on Pennsylvania) and brown 'Confederate Victory' diamonds on brown Confederate states, so they blend in. The casualty-size legend ends with '< 0'.
findings.why: Winner by colour is the one thing the sheet says to read from the diamonds. And a kid will ask how a battle had fewer than zero casualties.
findings.suggestion: Give the diamonds a thin white outline, and fix the smallest size label (I'd check the real break, probably 'fewer than 10,000').
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png; legend text 'Total casualties... < 0'.

findings.where: open and q2-dc views; legend panel and state labels; Q1 step 1, Q2 step 2
findings.what: At laptop size the legend lists battles and casualty sizes first. The five state groups Q1 needs start at the bottom edge and need scrolling, and the open panel covers New York and the coast. Zoomed to Washington, Maryland is the one neighbour without a label.
findings.why: Q1 begins with 'find the groups in the legend', and kids will think they aren't there.
findings.suggestion: Put U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) first in the legend, or shrink the casualty sizes, and make sure Maryland's label draws at the DC zoom.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--open.png (states section cut off at the bottom of the panel); --q2-dc.png (Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia, Delaware, District of Columbia labelled; Maryland not).

findings.where: q4-diamond view; Civil War Battlefields pop-up
findings.what: The Antietam pop-up shows the name twice and a broken picture, just a link reading 'American Battlefield Trust' where the image should be.
findings.why: It looks broken in front of the class. It may be the capture setup, so I'd check it on a school Chromebook.
findings.suggestion: Check the image link in the pop-up; if it fails on school devices, drop the image or use one hosted alongside the layer, and remove the repeated title.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q4-diamond.png, pop-up: 'Antietam / Antietam / ... American Battlefield Trust'.

the-battle-of-vicksburg.works: The map as it opens is close to ideal for Q1 to Q3: Vicksburg's yellow pin, all five labelled route pins, the railroad running from Monroe through Vicksburg to Jackson, and, with battlefields on, the May 1863 diamonds strung along that line. I could run the first three questions from the opening view with almost no preparation.

findings.where: q1-bookmark view; The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; Q1 step 1 and steps 3-4, Q2 (front step 1)
findings.what: The bookmark zooms in too far. Vicksburg is at the top edge, Milliken's Bend, Edwards and Jackson are off the screen, Bruinsburg Bend's label is cut off at the bottom, and modern highways fill the view.
findings.why: The sheet's first step makes the map worse than when it opened: kids can't find Jackson or follow the railroad to it, and two of the five route pins are gone.
findings.suggestion: Reset the bookmark to the opening view's extent (Monroe to Jackson, Milliken's Bend to Natchez), or drop step 1.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png and --q3-battles.png compared with --open.png.

findings.where: q4-porthudson view; basemap state labels and Civil War Battlefields; Q4 steps 2-4
findings.what: Zoomed out around Port Hudson, the only state name I can see is Alabama. Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas and Mississippi don't show (Louisiana may be under the pop-up). I didn't see the Memphis-to-Gulf zoom itself. There are eight or so unlabelled diamonds around Baton Rouge to click through to find Port Hudson.
findings.why: 'Read the state names on the basemap' doesn't work if the basemap doesn't show them. That's the evidence for the 'split the Confederacy' answer.
findings.suggestion: Add a 'Mississippi River, Memphis to the Gulf' bookmark at a zoom where the state names draw (or add a state-name label layer), and label Port Hudson.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q4-porthudson.png.

findings.where: open and q1-bookmark views; Railroads 1826 to 1911 legend and symbols; Q1 step 3
findings.what: The railroad legend lists Union Pacific, Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Southern Pacific and Central Pacific, none of which are anywhere near Vicksburg. The line kids need is called 'others'. In the bookmark view that line east of Vicksburg is a faint ticked line beside I-20, and the interstate is far more obvious.
findings.why: Kids will ask which of those railroads is Vicksburg's, and some will follow I-20 to Jackson instead of the railroad.
findings.suggestion: In this map, hide the transcontinental classes and rename 'others' to 'Railroads', and draw the railroad darker.
findings.evidence: Legend text (Union Pacific, Great Northern, ... others); the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png.

findings.where: open and q1-bookmark views; Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg; Q2 steps 1-2
findings.what: At the opening zoom, Milliken's Bend, Hard Times and Bruinsburg Bend sit right on the riverbank, so which side they're on is hard to judge. Zoomed in, the dashed state line loops through old river bends (New Carthage sits on one loop), and there's no Louisiana label. The pin is spelled 'Miliken's Bend'; the sheet says Milliken's.
findings.why: 'Which side of the river' is the key to Grant's route. Kids who misjudge a pin will get the whole idea of marching down the far bank wrong.
findings.suggestion: Label Louisiana and Mississippi on either side of the river at the opening zoom, and correct the pin name to Milliken's Bend.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--open.png ('Miliken's Bend' label, pins on the bank); --q1-bookmark.png (dashed loops around New Carthage).

findings.where: q3-battles view; Civil War Battlefields legend; Q3 and Q4
findings.what: Here Confederate Victory is a gray diamond, close to the gray 'Other' circle, and Inconclusive is the same yellow as the Vicksburg pin. On the Civil War Battlefields lesson map, the same layer uses brown for Confederate and white for Inconclusive.
findings.why: I'd teach these two lessons in the same unit. Kids who learned 'brown means Confederate' will misread this map.
findings.suggestion: Use the same symbols for Civil War Battlefields on both maps.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-battles.png legend; civil-war-battlefields--open.png legend.

findings.where: q3-championhill and q4-porthudson views; Civil War Battlefields pop-ups
findings.what: The pop-ups say 'Tap on image to view page', but there's no image, just a broken-picture link reading 'Battlefield Trust page'.
findings.why: It looks broken. It may be the capture setup, so I'd check it on a school Chromebook before class.
findings.suggestion: Check the image link; if it doesn't load on school devices, replace it with a plain text link.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-championhill.png and --q4-porthudson.png pop-ups.
